parts.title: The Clipper Races: an era of competition between cargo ships
parts.article:
The Clipper Races: an era of competition between cargo ships
 
(A) During the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries, the British East India Company had the monopoly on trade with China and India. This meant that because no rival could legally import tea or other goods from these countries at this time, the company was rarely in a hurry to transport its merchandise. Instead, its priority was to minimise costs by carrying as much as possible on each ship. This meant that its ships – known as East Indiamen – were enormous, strong and very slow.
 
(B) By 1800, the average East Indiaman could carry 1,200 tons of merchandise. The trading pattern for China tea usually meant the East Indiamen set sail from Britain in January, sailed round the Cape of Good Hope at the southernmost tip of Africa, and arrived in China in September. There they would load up that year's tea harvest, set off again and, depending on the wind and weather, aim to arrive back by the following September, so even with favourable sailing conditions, the round trip lasted almost two years, and if anything went wrong it could take a lot longer.
 
(C) However, by 1834 the company had lost its trading monopolies, and tea had become a freely traded item. Having no more use for its great ships, the company sold them off, and many were bought by merchants or their captains, who continued to plough the seas between Britain and China. But now that tea could be traded freely, a few smart sailors began to realise that whoever brought each new harvest of tea to Britain first stood to make the most money.
 
(D) This was partly because if you were home first, you could sell your shipment of tea before your competitors even arrived, and partly because consumers in Britain in the nineteenth century believed that the fresher and earlier-picked the tea, the better the resulting drink. Tea traders now needed faster, sleeker ships to bring their precious cargo back. Nevertheless, in Britain this idea only caught on slowly, and while the 1840s saw a few faster ships launched, for the time being many merchants remained satisfied with the slow but reliable East Indiamen.
 
(E) In fact it was the Americans who pioneered the first clipper ships. These vessels were fast and slender, with a narrow hull that was deeper at the back than at the front, and masses of sails on tall masts. They earned their name from the way that they 'clipped off' journey time. British merchants resolved to build their own clippers to rival the Americans, and the first British tea clipper, Stornaway, was built in Aberdeen in 1850. More tea clippers were designed and built in Britain throughout the 1850s and 1860s; they had a narrower beam than their American equivalents, making them less powerful during storms but faster in calmer weather.
 
(F) There was a great spirit of competition between the British and American ships plying the tea trade, but to begin with the Americans had the edge. Then in 1851 a British shipowner, Richard Green, built the aptly named clipper Challenger with the stated intention of beating the American ships. Loaded with tea, Challenger left China for London in 1852 at the same time as the American clipper Challenge, a much larger, older ship already greatly admired for its speed. Large sums were bet on which would complete the journey first. In the event, the British ship beat its rival to London by two days, amid much jubilation. From then on, such international races grew in popularity.
 
(G) After 1855, American participation in the British tea trade gradually stopped. But even without the Anglo-American rivalry, the competitive spirit continued. It was really ignited when new ports were opened up for trade in China. These included Foochow, which was much closer to the tea-producing areas than Canton, the port used previously. As a result, tea could be loaded on board earlier and fresher, and the clippers could set off in late May or early June – sometimes not even taking time to fill out the official paperwork – racing back to Britain whatever the difficulties.
 
(H) They sped down through the South China Sea and into the Indian Ocean, then raced to get round the southernmost tip of Africa at the Cape of Good Hope. Then it was north across the vast Atlantic, past the Azores, through the English Channel and into the estuary of the River Thames. Once there, they would be towed by tugs up the river and into the docks.
 
(I) The cargo of the winning ship could earn a premium of up to sixpence per pound – and so the captain and crew were rewarded by the owners of the cargo. But the races were about more than just money: the crews, about 40 men on each clipper, were expert sailors, proud of their ships, and they delighted in competing against each other. Without their enthusiasm, the races would never have happened, since getting home as fast as possible required the crew to be totally dedicated and to sacrifice much of their rest for the duration of the race.

questions.question: In the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries, the British East India Company faced a lot of competition.

analyses.content: 只要看到 "monopoly"（垄断）和 "no rival"（无对手）这两个词，就可以直接判定题目中的 "lot of competition" 是错的。
(Paragraph A) ...the British East India Company had the monopoly on trade with China and India. This meant that because no rival could legally import tea or other goods...
文章第一段明确说该公司拥有“垄断权”（monopoly），这意味着当时没有任何对手（no rival）可以合法进口货物，既然没对手，就不存在“激烈的竞争”。

questions.question: Before 1800, cargo size was the most important consideration for the East India Company.

analyses.content: 文章A段末尾提到，公司的首要任务（priority）是降低成本，方法就是每艘船尽可能多装货（carrying as much as possible），所以船都很大。
题目中的 "cargo size" 对应原文的 "carrying as much as possible"，"most important consideration" 对应原文的 "priority"。
(Paragraph A) Instead, its priority was to minimise costs by carrying as much as possible on each ship. This meant that its ships – known as East Indiamen – were enormous...

questions.question: At best, voyages of the East Indiamen to China and back took nearly two years to complete.

analyses.content: 文章B段说即使在有利的航行条件下（even with favourable sailing conditions），往返行程也要持续“将近两年”（almost two years）。
"At best"（在最好的情况下）对应原文的 "even with favourable sailing conditions"，"nearly" 对应 "almost"。
(Paragraph B) ...so even with favourable sailing conditions, the round trip lasted almost two years...

questions.question: Before 1834, voyages to and from China were considered to be highly dangerous.

analyses.content: 文章虽然提到如果出问题时间会更长，也提到了可能会遇到的天气，但并没有明确指出这种航行被认为是“高度危险的”（highly dangerous）。
不要自己脑补古代航海肯定危险，雅思阅读里没写“dangerous”或者相关形容词，就不能选True。
(Paragraph B) ...and if anything went wrong it could take a lot longer. (文中只提到了时间变长，没提危险程度。)

questions.question: After 1834, the ships which had served the East India Company stopped being used for commercial purposes.

analyses.content: 文章C段说这些大船被卖给了其他商人和船长，他们继续用这些船在英国和中国之间“航行经商”（continued to plough the seas），并没有停止商业用途。
看到 "sold them off" 别以为就是报废了，后面紧接着说它们被买走并继续使用。
(Paragraph C) ...the company sold them off, and many were bought by merchants or their captains, who continued to plough the seas between Britain and China.

questions.question: In the nineteenth century, British drinkers preferred tea made from mature leaves to that made from younger leaves.

analyses.content: (Paragraph D) ...consumers in Britain in the nineteenth century believed that the fresher and earlier-picked the tea, the better the resulting drink.
文章D段提到消费者认为茶采摘得越早（earlier-picked），味道越好，也就是说他们喜欢嫩叶（younger），而不是题目说的老叶子（mature）。
题目中的 "mature"（成熟/老）和原文的 "earlier-picked"（早采/嫩）是反义关系。

analyses.content: 定位到E段，文中描述美国快船有高高的桅杆和大量的 "sails"（帆），这里的 "masses of" 对应题目中的 "number of"。
(Paragraph E) These vessels were fast and slender, with a narrow hull... and masses of sails on tall masts.
定位到E段末尾，文中说英国船比美国的窄，这导致它们在 "storms"（风暴）中动力不足，表现受到影响。
(Paragraph E) ...making them less powerful during storms but faster in calmer weather.
定位到F段，文中提到Richard Green建造了一艘叫 "Challenger" 的船，并成功击败了美国对手。
注意不要填成美国的船名 "Challenge"，只差一个字母 "r"，英国赢的那艘叫 "Challenger"。
(Paragraph F) Then in 1851 a British shipowner, Richard Green, built the aptly named clipper Challenger with the stated intention of beating the American ships.
(Paragraph G) It was really ignited when new ports were opened up for trade in China.
定位到G段，文中提到当新的 "ports"（港口）在中国开放贸易时，竞争真正被点燃了（ignited）。
定位到G段末尾，文中说船长们太急了，有时甚至没时间去填写官方的 "paperwork"（文件/手续）。
(Paragraph G) ...sometimes not even taking time to fill out the official paperwork – racing back to Britain whatever the difficulties.
定位到H段最后一句，船到达泰晤士河口后，会被 "tugs"（拖船）拖进码头。
(Paragraph H) Once there, they would be towed by tugs up the river and into the docks.
定位到I段，文中提到船员被奖励，但比赛不仅仅是为了 "money"（钱），说明钱是一个动力，热情是另一个动力。
虽然文中用了 "rewarded"，但题目结构是 "motivated by both X and Y"，对应原文 "more than just money... enthusiasm"，所以填 "money"。
(Paragraph I) But the races were about more than just money: the crews... delighted in competing against each other.
